text.p: --BIRTHDAYS--

Political maverick JOHN WILKES was born in London in 1727. He was credited with the famous riposte to LORD SANDWICH when asked "Will you die of a pox or on the gallows?". WILKES reportedly replied "That depends, my Lord, on whether I embrace your lordship's mistress or your lordship's principles." WILKES campaigned for press freedom and was elected to Parliament four times but not allowed to take his seat until 1774.
Queensland politician RATCLIFFE PRING was born in 1825. He resigned after starting a drunken brawl in the Legislative Assembly. He was later appointed as a judge.
Australian provincial newspaper pioneer EDWARD STEPHENS was born in 1846.
Danish author BARONESS KAREN BLIXEN, wrote "Out of Africa" under the pseudonym of ISAK DINESEN, was born in 1885.
American novelist NATHANIEL WEST, whose "Lonelyhearts" was made into a film, was born in 1903. He drew a scathing picture of Hollywood in "The Day of the Locust".
Playwright ARTHUR MILLER was born in Manhattan in 1915. His works include the "Death of a Salesman".
Australian author SUMNER LOCKE ELIOT was born in 1917. His play "Rusty Bugles" was banned.
Actress RITA HAYWORTH was born in 1918. She partnered FRED ASTAIRE in "You Were Never Lovelier" and caused a sensation in "Gilda".
American actor MONTGOMERY CLIFT, whose films included "From Here To Eternity" and "The Misfits", was born in 1920.
American stuntman who specialised in leaping over rows of cars or buses on a motorcycle, EVEL KNIEVEL, was born in 1939.

United States guitarist, saxophonist, violinist and singer, JAMES SEALS, was born in 1941. He formed the duo "Seals and Crofts" and their hits included "Summer Breeze" (1972), "Diamond Girl" (1973) and "Get Closer" (1976).
--EVENTS--
1806 : The first black ruler of Haiti, the tyrannical
Emperor JACQUES I, was assassinated.
1854 : The siege of Sebastopol (Sevastopol) began at
which 60,000 troops besieged and finally (11 months later) took the main Russian naval base of the Black Sea fleet.
1906 : The first telegraph picture was transmitted over

more than one thousand miles by German professor ARTHUR KORN. The invention allowed newspapers to publish pictures taken only hours earlier on the other side of the world. The invention involved taking a photograph a small part at a time and producing an electrical current corresponding to its shade of grey.
1908 : A tuberculosis serum was developed by France's
Professor LANNELONGUE.
1915 : Victoria Crosses were awarded to eight Australians
and one New Zealander for heroism at Gallipoli.
1927 : Oil was discovered at Roma in western Queensland.
Oil gushed from the bore at a rate of 50 gallons an hour.
1934 : HITLER cut income tax for large families.
1944 : The Sydney newspaper strike ended when 2,500
members from 14 unions went back to work.
1955 : Australia's Governor-General SIR WILLIAM SLIM said
"something should be done about Australia's flies."
1956 : Britain's first nuclear power station, CALDER
HALL, was opened by the Queen.
1967 : Australia's prime minister HAROLD HOLT announced
Australia would send reinforcements to Vietnam, taking to eight-thousand the number of men in the overseas force.
1972 : The Queen arrived in Yugoslavia on a State visit,
the first to a Communist state by a British monarch.
1973 : Arab oil producers increased oil prices and cut
back production in response to U.S. support of Israel in the Yom Kippur war.
1985 : The House of Lords voted to allow doctors to
prescribe contraceptives to girls under the age of 16 without parental consent. Catholic mother Mrs VICTORIA GILLICK campaigned unsuccessfully against the move.
1989 : The global ban on ivory trading was ratified by
the Endangered Species convention.
1994 : Jordan and Israel initialled an historic peace
treaty, cementing an end to their 46-year state of war.
1994 : U.N. mediators said the Angolan government and
UNITA rebels had reached agreement in principle to end nearly 20 years of civil war.
